title: "3.2 Pressure Integrals"
---

{{< include ../_checkpoint-widget.qmd >}}

## The big idea

Submerged objects will experience forces due to pressure. A notable consequence is the **buoyant force**, which explains why objects can float in water. Beyond that we also can ask questions like: how much force is being experienced by a dam? How much torque does it take to hold a submerged gate closed? We will build up to a fairly general equation for evaluating (vector) forces on surfaces due to pressure (completing this discussion in the next reading). You'll need to remember some Calc 3, but I'll walk you through it!

## Think first

**Recall**

1. What's the equation for hydrostatic pressure as a function of depth? Why doesn't it depend on the width or length of the container?
2. If you plotted pressure vs. depth for a pool, what would that plot look like?

**Look ahead**

1. For a vertical wall holding back water of depth $H$, do you expect the total force to scale with $H$ or $H^2$?
2. Does a gate leaning at an angle take *more*, the *same*, or *less* force to hold shut than a vertical gate of the same height?
3. If we are going to integrate pressure over area to get force, what information do we need to know to calculate that integral?


## Forces from pressure distributions

### Horizontal surfaces

Let's imagine a rectangular pool, width $W$, length $L$, depth $H$, filled with a fluid of density $\rho$, and gravity $g$ is a thing. **What is the total force on the bottom of the pool?** We need simply to calculate the weight of the fluid: $F= mg = \rho WLH g$.

We can also think about this via the pressure on the bottom of the pool: from hydrostatics, the pressure is $\rho g H$, and then the total area of the bottom of the pool is $WL$, so the total force (i.e., the weight) is $F=\rho g WLH$... same answer!

This gives us a hint about how we will calculate forces on submerged bodies: we will look at the pressure on the object, then multiply by area (in a calculus-sensitive way) to get total force.

### Vertical surfaces

Vertical walls have an added complication: the pressure varies with depth, and so it is not just $(\text{force})=(\text{constant pressure})(\text{area})$. Pressure is $p(y)=\rho g y$, and $y$ changes over the surface... we are going to need to **integrate pressure over area**. It will look something like this:

$$
F_x =\int p(y) dA.
$$

::: {.column-margin}
The dimensions of a differential area $dA$ are still L² and the integral symbol $\int$ has no dimensions... it basically means "sum". So $\int p dA$ has dimensions of force.
:::



::: {.callout-important}
This is an applied math class... we need to figure out how to apply math to this situation! Our goal is to evaluate this integral based on engineering parameters in the problem.

- We have our integrand: $p(y)=\rho g y$.
- The area we are integrating over can be described with coordinates $y$ and $z$. Thus, we can write $dA = dy dz$.
- We need to set the bounds of integration. If the pool depth is $H$ and width is $W$, we can say that one integral goes from $y=0$ to $y=H$ and the other from $z=0$ to $z=W$.

Populating:

$$
F_x =\int\limits_0^W\int\limits_0^H \rho g y \,dy dz.
$$

::: {.column-margin}
You have to learn how to assemble integrals like this yourself!
:::

:::

We can evaluate this integral. Since the integrand does not depend on $z$, and since $\rho g$ is constant:


$$
F_x =\rho g \int\limits_0^W dz \int\limits_0^H y \,dy = \rho g W \left(\frac{H^2}{2}\right).
$$

There it is: the total force on the wall, acting to the right!

A couple things worth noting:

- The average pressure is $p_\text{avg}=\rho g H/2$... the pressure halfway down. The total force is the average pressure times the total area.
- The bottom half of the pool experiences more force than the top. This means the location where the effective force is acting is going to be more than $H/2$ deep. This is relevant for torque calculations — more on this later!

Let's add another complication: suppose the wall is at an angle of $\beta$ with respect to the vertical. (Above we did the $\beta=0$ case.) What is the force now? 

Let's try to build it up as an integral again, but now our differential area $dA$ is not simply $dy dz$... we aren't just varying $y$ as we move across the surface. Define our position along the wall as $y'$, and we'll then have $\cos\beta = y/y'$. So $y'=0$ at the top of the wall and $y'=H/\cos\beta$ at the bottom of the wall.

```{=html}
<div style="display:flex; justify-content:center; margin: 1.5em 0;">
<svg width="260" height="200" viewBox="0 0 260 200" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="sans-serif">
  <rect x="0" y="0" width="260" height="200" fill="#ffffff"/>

  <!-- right triangle: vertical leg y, hypotenuse y', angle beta between them at the top -->
  <polygon points="170,30 170,150 114,150" fill="none" stroke="#1a1a1a" stroke-width="1.5"/>

  <path d="M 170 48 A 18 18 0 0 1 162 46" fill="none" stroke="#1a1a1a" stroke-width="1.2"/>
  <text x="158" y="60" font-size="15" font-style="italic" fill="#1a1a1a">&#946;</text>

  <text x="182" y="94" font-size="16" font-style="italic" fill="#1a1a1a">y</text>

  <text x="118" y="80" font-size="16" font-style="italic" fill="#1a1a1a">y&#8242;</text>
</svg>
</div>
```

::: {.callout-tip}
The benefit of this approach: it is intuitive to write the integral. There is a way to solve this problem using $dA = dy dz$ (I think), but it is not obvious to me at all. With the approach we are developing here, the differential area in our integral is just $dA=dy'dz$ and the bounds on $y'$ are $0\rightarrow H/\cos\beta$ (and $z$ is still $0\rightarrow W$). We have to do some setup work, but the integral we create will be easy to comprehend.
:::

Now we are integrating with respect to $y'$ and $z$, and so our integrand needs to be written in terms of $y'$ (instead of $y$). No problem, we can make the substitution described above: $p=\rho g y = \rho g \cos\beta y'$.

At last:

$$
F =\int\limits_0^W\int\limits_0^{H/\cos\beta} \rho g \cos\beta y' \,dy' dz.
$$

which we can integrate. One last note: at every location on the surface, the force due to pressure points in the same direction: $\hat{n}= \left\langle \cos\beta, -\sin\beta \right\rangle$. This means the total force points in that direction as well.


::: {.callout-tip}
I am never comfortable with the initial definition of $\hat{n}$. Here's a tip on how to check it: explore a couple cases of $\beta$ and make sure they match up with expectations.

In the case where $\beta=0$, the force points in the $+\hat{x}$-direction. Indeed: $\hat{n}= \left\langle \cos\beta, -\sin\beta \right\rangle=\left\langle 1,0\right\rangle$. In the case where $\beta = \pi/4$, it points in the $\left\langle 1, -1 \right\rangle$ direction. Indeed: $\hat{n}= \left\langle \cos\beta, -\sin\beta \right\rangle=\left\langle \sqrt{2}/{2},-\sqrt{2}/{2}\right\rangle$. (Same direction, just normalized.)
:::

```{=html}
  <path d="M220,50 l5,-5 l5,5 l5,-5 l5,5" fill="none" stroke="#333" stroke-width="1.3"/>

  <!-- angled wall (the gate): hinged at its base, leaning to the right by beta, its outer corner touching the image edge -->
  <polygon points="250,256 330,85 344,92 264,263" fill="#6b6b6b" stroke="#1a1a1a" stroke-width="1.5"/>

  <!-- reference vertical (the beta=0 wall) and angle marker, at the top of the gate, inside the new triangle -->
  <line x1="344" y1="92" x2="344" y2="150" stroke="#888" stroke-width="1.2" stroke-dasharray="4,3"/>
  <path d="M 344 122 A 30 30 0 0 0 331 119" fill="none" stroke="#1a1a1a" stroke-width="1.3"/>
  <text x="327" y="141" font-size="16" font-style="italic" fill="#1a1a1a">&#946;</text>

  <!-- the gate: a hatch about 1/3 of the way down the wall, 1/3 the wall's length -->
  <polygon points="303,142 277,199 291,206 317,149" fill="#c0392b" stroke="#1a1a1a" stroke-width="1.5"/>

  <!-- hinge at the bottom of the gate, slightly wider than the wall is thick -->
  <circle cx="284" cy="203" r="10" fill="#c0392b" stroke="#1a1a1a" stroke-width="1.5"/>
</svg>

```


Let's add a final complication: suppose the angled wall has a gate with length $\ell$, and its hinge is located at a certain depth $H_\text{hinge}$. **How much torque is necessary to keep it closed?**

First: what is a torque? We need to keep track of our displacement from the hinge (the lever arm) and the force, and luckily, in this geometry, those things are perpendicular. 

::: {.column-margin}
More generally we'll have the torque vector $\mathbf{M}= \mathbf{r}\times \mathbf{F}$. We'll see this next reading.
:::

Similar to with the pressure integral, we need to sum together the contributions of torque at each point on the gate. The force will be $p dA$, and so the total torque will be

$$
M = \int r(y) p(y) dA.
$$

where $r(y)$ is the displacement from the hinge. If we define the same $y'$ as above, how can we describe our position along the gate in terms of $y'$? Start by recognizing that the hinge is located at $y'=H_\text{hinge}/\cos\beta$. Then, on the gate, our distance from the hinge is $r(y') = H_\text{hinge}/\cos\beta - y'$. Thus we can populate our integral

$$
M =\int\limits_0^W\int\limits_{{H_\text{hinge}/\cos\beta}-\ell}^{H_\text{hinge}/\cos\beta} \left(H_\text{hinge}/\cos\beta - y'\right)\left(\rho g \cos\beta y'\right) \,dy' dz.
$$





## Curved surfaces

::: {.callout-important}
Don't forget that force is a **vector** while pressure is a **scalar**. In the case of a flat wall, the force from pressure acts normal to the surface, and so the total force will act normal to the surface as well. If a wall is curved, the pressure acts normal to the surface *at every point*, but not every point has the same surface normal! And so the description of the total force is more complicated.

We'll cover this in the next reading.
:::
